entries.title: Chicago area voters 'hope for the best' during 2026 midterm election
entries.summary: <p>Months after immigration enforcement upended her neighborhood, Little Village resident Alex Cortez said the community is still trying to heal from the trauma.</p><p>Rather than wait and hope for change, Cortez decided to take action, casting her ballot Tuesday morning in her first midterm election.</p><p>“It's been very difficult,” said Cortez, 35. “What the [Trump] administration did was traumatic and it hurt our community.”</p><p>On Sept. 8, 2025, the Trump administration launched <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/immigration/2026/midway-blitz-by-the-numbers/" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>, a deportation campaign that brought hundreds of federal agents to the Chicago area and resulted in nearly 4,000 arrests.</p><p>Cortez said she had voted in previous presidential elections but had never participated in other elections. Now, she said, she realizes that every election, including midterm elections, matters. </p><p>She was among the first voters to cast a ballot Tuesday morning at Madero Middle School, 3202 W. 28th St., as Chicagoans headed to the polls for the 2026 general election.</p><p>Cortez said the effects of the administration’s immigration enforcement actions were not the only challenges facing her community. She said residents were also struggling with rising costs, and hoped to see more resources for local schools and efforts to reduce street gang violence.</p><p>“I came out here and cast my vote for entries.title: Jessica Dixon Heitman takes early lead in suburban statehouse race spurred by scandal
entries.summary: <p>Early returns Tuesday night showed a race that's still too close to call for a far southwest suburban General Assembly district — a contest that could provide an indicator of how much Springfield’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>latest sexual harassment scandal</u></a> is impacting super-majority Democrats in the Illinois General Assembly and House Speaker Emanuel “Chris” Welch’s leadership of his chamber.</p><p>Democratic state Rep. Jessican Dixon Heitman, D-Plainfield was appointed to fill the 97th House District seat after former state Rep. Harry Benton resigned. She led with about 69% of the vote over Republican nominee Gabby Shanahan, with about 31%. But that's with only about 30% of expected votes counted so far.</p><p>The race would’ve been hotly contested even if Benton hadn’t been forced out amid allegations of misconduct over the summer.</p><p>But the contest in a rare purple district on Illinois’ grossly gerrymandered political map was tossed higher into the air over the summer with Benton’s resignation — which raised the broader question of why Welch backed Benton's 2024 reelection bid despite being aware of a preceding complaint against Benton at that time.</p><p>Shanahan, making <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/16/illinois-house-district-97-election-shanahan-heitman-benton-sexual-harassment-scandal" target="_blank" ><u>a second run for the office</u></a> she lost to Benton in 2024 by just four percentage points, was sunk in no small part by the $1.4 million Welch directed to Benton’s campaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div </div> </div><p>This time Shanahan’s up against Dixon Heitman, the Plainfield Democrat whose campaign has received support from the Welch-controlled Democrats for the Illinois House political committee to the tune of more than $1.6 million.</p><p>Dixon Heitman herself saw “red flags” in Benton’s office during a brief stint as a contract employee, she has said, but didn’t make a formal complaint.</p><p>Dixon Heitman, a granddaughter of the late former U.S. Sen. Alan Dixon, told the <a class="Link" href="https://fwrnews.com/2026/07/21/38732/" target="_blank" ><u>Farmers Weekly Review of Will County</u></a> that she respected the wishes of the young complainant who “was very opposed to filing any sort of report.”</p><p>Welch’s office was aware of allegations surfacing from Benton’s office, but he has claimed no choice but to continue backing Benton without a formal complaint to spur an investigation.</p><p>The speaker booted Benton from the caucus this February when another woman filed a complaint. A third woman’s complaint was detailed in a legislative watchdog’s report that prompted Benton to step down. He has denied wrongdoing.</p><p>Shanahan has said Dixon Heitman should’ve done more to flag Benton’s alleged misbehavior, while Illinois Republicans across the board have lambasted Welch’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/05/welch-benton-harassment-working-group-cassidy" target="_blank" ><u>handling of the case</u></a> in addition to his own social media interactions. He has apologized for messages sent to a Benton complainant after the fact that left her uncomfortable.</p><p>Shanahan also called on Dixon Heitman to pledge not to vote for Welch as speaker when the new General Assembly is sworn in next year.</p><p>Watching election results roll in with Will County Democrats at IBEW Local 176 in Joliet, Dixon Heitman said she hasn’t yet considered who should hold the gavel.</p><p>“I've been so focused on campaigning and being in my district, I haven't given it much thought yet,” she said. “It's something that I really have to sit down and do pros and cons and really think about it.”</p><p>While state Rep. Kelly Cassidy, D-Chicago, has slammed Welch over the case, no Democratic representatives have publicly called for him to give up the gavel. Several representatives declined to join a sexual harassment working group assembled by Welch to address the issue.</p><p>Welch himself took the speaker’s office in the wake of ex-House Speaker Michael Madigan’s downfall, which was precipitated by his own mishandling of sexual harassment allegations in his 13th Ward political organization almost a decade ago.</p><p>Still, Shanahan and Dixon Heitman, both working moms, agreed Springfield’s troubling culture of sexual harassment wasn’t the top issue for voters in a district spanning most of Plainfield, part of Joliet and smaller portions of Aurora, Naperville, Bolingbrook, Oswego and Shorewood.</p><p>As in most races this season, the most pressing concern was the rapidly rising cost of living, both candidartes said.</p><p>“People are looking for somebody that is going to represent them both in the district and in Springfield, but also someone that they know that they can reach out to at any time,” said Dixon Heitman, a former media relations consultant. “That is something that I have been running on my platform constantly: transparency, honesty, being readily available to my community at any time.”</p><p>“You have a broad range of people that really want to be able to afford to live in the 97th District,” Shanahan, a court-appointed special advocate for children in the Kendall County court system, told the Sun-Times before Election Day. “They need their property tax crisis address. They need the cost of living address, and they want somebody that is going to represent them with integrity and honesty.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-7d0000" name="module-7d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b><u>Race Results</u></b><br><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/governor-illinois-jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-results" >Illinois Governor</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-senate-illinois-midterm-results" >U.S. Senate</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-house-illinois-midterm-results" >4th Congressional District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-state-comptroller-attorney-general-secretary-of-state" >Illinois State Offices</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-illinois-house-97-midterm-results" >Illinois’ 97th House District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-house-midterm-results" >Illinois General Assembly</a></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Chicago School Board Election 2026: The citywide race for president
entries.summary: <p>Former CPS principal and current school board member Jessica Biggs was leading Tuesday with 50% of the vote, with 61% of the precincts reporting in the city-wide race to become the first-ever elected president of the Chicago School Board, but there is no clear winner yet, according to results from the Associated Press.</p><p>Chicago Teachers Union-backed Hilario Dominguez was trailing Biggs with 30% of the vote, and attorney Victor Henderson had 17%. Sendhil Revuluri, a leadership consultant who suspended his campaign in September, had 3%.</p><p>The person elected to this powerful, but unpaid position, will work with 20 other members to set a vision and goals for CPS for the next four years. They will represent the board publicly, run the board’s monthly meetings and help set the agenda for a body that oversees a roughly $10 billion annual budget.</p><p>A vast majority of the money that flooded the school board election has focused on the race given the president’s influence. Of the more than <a class="Link" href="https://graphics-stage.suntimes.com/esb/school-board/money/#mm-president" target="_blank" ><u>$8.3 million raised directly by the candidates</u></a>, $5.2 million has been collected in the president’s race, including by two candidates who withdrew. Biggs raised nearly $1.9 million, Dominguez $1.7 million and Henderson about $700,000 — nearly all of that money he loaned himself.</p><p>When spending by super PACs, which can’t coordinate with candidates, is factored in, $13.9 million<b> </b>has been spent supporting or opposing candidates, according to an analysis by the Sun-Times and WBEZ.</p><p>This includes $3.5 million<b> </b>to oppose Dominguez by groups that don’t want the CTU’s candidate to lead the board. PACs funded by the CTU have spent just $577,000 in support of his campaign.</p><p>One of the first tasks for whomever takes over as board president in January — and the board they will lead — could be dealing with a significant budget shortfall. This year’s budget is counting on Springfield in a veto session later this month extra funding to balance the budget. entries.title: Patty García wins Illinois' 4th Congressional District race for ‘Chuy’ García's congressional seat
entries.summary: <p>After months of swatting away criticism over her surprise candidacy for Illinois’ 4th Congressional District, Patty García claimed victory in the race to replace her former boss: U.S. Rep. Jesus “Chuy” García.</p><p>With 28% percent of votes in, Patty García led 70.6% to GOP candidate Lupe Castillo with 15.1% and independent candidate Chris Getty with 10.5%. Working Class Party candidate Ed Hershey had 3.8% of the vote, according to the Associated Press. </p><p>There has been no shortage of controversy in the race, where “Chuy” García’s last-minute decision to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2025/11/03/jesus-chuy-garcia-reelection-dropping-out-chief-of-staff-running" target="_blank" ><u>drop out of the primary race</u></a> led him to helping his chief of staff quickly take his spot on the primary ballot.</p><p>But Patty García ignored the noise and built major Democratic support, both in Illinois and in Washington. And while she repeatedly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/07/21/patty-garcia-4th-congressional-district-midterm-election-ballot-challenges" target="_blank" ><u>defended the ballot switch</u></a>, which the congressman attributed to family and health reasons, she has also asserted that voters were focused on other pressing issues, including constituents who were hit hard by Operation Midway Blitz and others who are struggling to make ends meet.</p><p>She was fully embraced by Illinois Democrats after the primary, spending time campaigning with Gov. JB Pritzker and other top Democrats. She also campaigned with Congressman García, who heaped praise on her.</p><p>Patty García also racked up more than 175 endorsements from Democrats, including U.S. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Lt. Gov Juliana Stratton and Rep. Delia Ramirez. She’s also backed by the Illinois AFL-CIO, Chicago Federation of Labor and SEIU Illinois State Council.</p><p>In announcing her run, the 41-year-old, who has worked in Chuy García office since 2019, vowed to continue his work fighting for immigrant and working-class families in the Southwest Side district that stretches to the western suburbs.</p><p>“My mother crossed the border, undocumented, and pregnant with me. And she arrived in Chicago wearing sandals in the middle of the winter because she didn’t know about the icy, cold Chicago,” said Patty García, who has a Ph.D. in education policy. “Today, families dressed like ours are facing a new kind of ICE, an assault on immigrants that threatens everything we’ve built. That’s why I’m running for Congress.”</p><p>She put a profane exclamation mark on her candidacy after saying President Donald Trump “has declared war on our community, on my community, on my neighbors, on my family, on the Fourth District.</p><p>“And let me be clear: f--- ICE,” she said.</p><p>During the general election, Patty García — no relation to the congressman — also fended off <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/01/28/chuy-garcia-congress-seat-byron-sigcho-lopez-mayra-macias-independent-bids" target="_blank" ><u>two independent candidates</u></a> who railed on what they called a Democratic machine play, but ultimately failed to survive petition challenges with the Illinois State Board of Elections.</p><p>Getty has served as mayor of Lyons since 2009 and is also the supervisor of Lyons Township. He’s also a licensed insurance producer. Getty said he ran to improve the cost of living and to focus on immigration, public safety and government accountability.</p><p>Getty in November wrote a scorching Chicago Tribune op-ed piece criticizing Congressman García for his last-minute decision not to run — and perhaps setting the stage for his own candidacy.</p><p>“It’s a move right out of the playbook of machine politics, anointing successors rather than letting the democratic process determine them,” Getty wrote in the piece.</p><p>Getty, who was elected mayor in 2009 at the age of 26, said he thought being from the suburbs could be seen as a strength in the district that has traditionally been represented by Chicagoans.</p><p>Castillo ran on a platform of “pro-family values and policies.” She said she was the only candidate who “will protect women’s sports and girl’s bathrooms,” and who would support law enforcement over criminals. She was also supportive of voter ID and school choice. She has lived in the district for 43 years.</p><p>Congressman García's decision in November to drop out of the race shook up Illinois politics last year. Along with his decision to retire, the state saw four open congressional seats and the open Senate race to replace U.S. Sen. entries.title: Syed leads Hills in one of the most expensive Illinois legislative races ever
entries.summary:
On a night when Republicans were not expected to make much of a dent into Democrats' supermajority in the Illinois General Assembly Tuesday, a pair of closely watched races were shaping up to be too close to call.

In one key race, state Rep. Nabeela Syed, a Democrat from Inverness, is challenging incumbent Republican Darby Hills of Barrington Hills for the Illinois Senate 26th District seat.

With 23% of the votes counted, Syed led Hills with almost 58% of the vote.

The $6.5 million raised makes it one of the most expensive contests in the history of the General Assembly, said Alisa Kaplan, executive director of Reform for Illinois.

Syed received at least $4.7 million in contributions, much of it from her party, while Hills has raised $1.8 million, said Kaplan, whose organization runs the Illinois Sunshine Database.

"The Democratic leadership wants to flip this seat, and it shows," Kaplan said.

Syed raised more than $3 million from the Democratic Party of Illinois and the Illinois Senate Democratic Fund, which is controlled by Illinois Senate President Don Harmon. She’s also raised substantial amounts of money from unions.

Hills' last big contribution from her party was in August when the Illinois Senate Republican Campaign gave her $300,000.

Separate from Hills' own fundraising, a political action committee called the Strong Independent Leadership Committee formed last month to oppose Syed. It’s stated purpose is “ensuring only strong, independent leaders are elected by opposing extreme candidates,” according to a state filing.

Vince Foglia of North Barrington formed the political committee and contributed $500,000 to it.

Separately, Foglia and his family have also contributed $500,000 to Hills’ campaign.

The northwest suburban district includes parts of Cook, Lake, McHenry and Kane counties.

Hills was appointed to fill out the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization.

Syed, 27, is completing her second term in the Illinois House after graduating from the University of California Berkeley in 2021, while Hills is completing the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization. Syed was the youngest woman and one of the only Muslims ever to be elected to the Illinois General Assembly.

Hills, 50, has raised Syed’s youth and experience as a campaign issue. In the final days, she’s called Syed “too extreme” to represent her district.

"I've represented the community for four years," Syed said in an interview. "I'm proud of my record. It's disingenuous to call that extreme."

Some Syed supporters took exception to the "too extreme" remark.

"It comes from a place of desperation," Syed supporter Rija Arshad said Tuesday night. "There's nothing else to hit Nabeela on because she's strong on her issues."

A former prosecutor and 2021 Mrs. Illinois America, Hills was a village trustee before being appointed to McConchie’s seat. She has campaigned for public safety, especially related to children, lower taxes and government spending controls.

Syed, a Palatine native, said affordability and access to health care are among her top priorities.

Both candidates call for more oversight of data center development, a contentious issue across the state.

While Democrats see a potential to pick up suburban seats it only pads the big advantages they already have in the legislature.

Before Tuesday’s election, Democrats hold super-majorities in both the Illinois House (78-40) and Illinois Senate (40-19). Every Illinois House seat was up for election Nov. 3, while voters were slated to decide 39 state senate races, two thirds of the total members.

Elsewhere, Democrats were looking to unseat 52nd House District Republican Martin McLaughlin who faced Maria Peterson again.

With 24% of votes counted, Peterson led with 57% to 43% for McLaughlin.

In 2024, McLaughlin eked out a victory against Peterson, beating her by fewer than 50 votes.

Peterson cited affordability, environmental protection and safety atop of the issues she was focusing on, and pointed to her records as a lawyer doing advocacy work.

McLaughlin has said he’s focused on government spending and accountability.

More than a quarter of the members of the Illinois General Assembly represent Chicago or portions of the city, and the vast majority are Democrats.

Only one incumbent Democrat lost in March. State Rep. Jaime Andrade Jr. was beat in his primary for House District 40 by challenger and community activist Miguel Alvelo Rivera for the North Side seat. Alvelo Rivera is unopposed in Tuesday’s election.

Republicans saw an opportunity in another rematch where Republican Liz Bishop was challenging incumbent Democrat Amy “Murri” Briel in the 76th Illinois House District race in north central Illinois. The campaign includes some eyebrow-raising allegations.

However, Briel was leading with 66% after 19% of the votes were counted.

Bishop, who lost to Briel in 2024 by less than 600 votes, released a recorded interview with a former staffer who alleged that Briel sexually harassed her, fed her prescription stimulant drugs and smoked pot while working as a lawmaker.

Briel denied the allegations and said a state legislative watchdog investigation concluded the claims were unfounded.

entries.title: Election Day ‘glitch’ leads to long lines, ballot issues at Chicago voting sites
entries.summary: <p>Election Day in Chicago did not go completely smoothly for some voters at multiple polling sites on Tuesday. </p><p>One of the two precincts at Holstein Park reportedly had been without paper ballots for hours Tuesday evening and had only one voting machine, creating a long line, a Chicago Sun-Times reporter observed.</p><p>The Chicago Board of Elections said it provided ballots and touchscreen voting machines at Holstein Park, 1st Ward and District 4 sites that were affected, according to board representative Julie Metea.</p><p>She explained the cause was related to split precincts with multiple ballot combinations.</p><p>"The issue appeared to be in those split precincts where there are several different ballot combinations and styles, because maybe one half of the precinct's voting on one congressional district, another one's voting on another one. So they may have as many as seven ballot combinations," Metea said.</p><p>Metea indicated election board officials did not know how many other voting sites or precincts might have been affected, she said.</p><p>“We want to apologize to voters who came out and encountered a glitch,” Metea said. “Their votes are important. We value their time, and we apologize for the inconvenience as we're investigating and fulfilling the ballot need.”</p>

entries.title: La demócrata Juliana Stratton toma las riendas de Dick Durbin tras una victoria decisiva en el Senado
entries.summary: <p>El enérgico mensaje de Juliana Stratton contra el presidente Trump la ayudó a conseguir una contundente victoria sobre el republicano Don Tracy por el escaño abierto en el Senado para reemplazar al senador Dick Durbin.</p><p>La Associated Press declaró a Stratton ganadora cuando las urnas cerraron a las 7 p.m.</p><p>Stratton, de 61 años, también hizo historia al convertirse en la segunda mujer negra en representar a Illinois en el Senado de Estados Unidos.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-810000" name="module-810000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>En Stratton, los votantes de Illinois eligieron una voz progresista con un lema de campaña de "F*** Trump" para tomar las riendas de Durbin, el senador de mayor antigüedad que ocupaba el escaño desde 1996. Stratton, compañera de fórmula del gobernador JB Pritzker desde 2018, prometió repetidamente que se enfrentaría al presidente, y su campaña en las primarias ayudó a energizar a los votantes en una contienda de 10 candidatos.</p><p>Ahora llevará a Washington, D.C. su plataforma progresista para abolir el Servicio de Inmigración yControl de Aduanas(ICE) e impulsar un salario mínimo de $25 la hora, junto a cinco nuevos colegas demócratas en el Congreso, parte de una nueva ola de la delegación de Illinois en el Congreso tras una serie de renuncias y movimientos este año.</p><p>En el lado suroeste de Chicago, los simpatizantes llenaron el Ramova Theatre para una fiesta de vigilia electoral parecida a una salida nocturna en un club. Fueron recibidos por un animado DJ que pinchaba remixes de música pop mientras esperaban el discurso de victoria de Stratton.</p><p>Varios bares ofrecieron cerveza, vino y seltzer gratis, con una barra de pago para cócteles y bebidas con 5 mg de THC. Varios letreros de campaña esparcidos por el teatro decían "Denle al pueblo lo que quiere" y "Mujeres negras por Juliana".</p><p>Pritzker ha restado importancia a su papel en la ayuda a Stratton, incluyendo una abultada contribución de $10 millones a la campaña primaria que le permitió emitir anuncios en televisión. Pero el gobernador ahora puede jactarse de haber ayudado a elegir a una aliada cercana para el Senado de Estados Unidos.</p><p>Stratton, exmediadora, fue elegida por primera vez para la Cámara de Representantes de Illinois en 2016. Como vicegobernadora, ayudó a liderar la Iniciativa por la Equidad en el Nacimiento, que abordó la disparidad racial en las tasas de mortalidad materna entre las mujeres negras en Illinois. También encabezó la Iniciativa de Justicia, Equidad y Oportunidad, con el objetivo de orientar el sistema penal estatal hacia programas más restaurativos.</p><p>Su trabajo con la Iniciativa Ag Connects Us All, que destacó cómo la industria agrícola podía abordar las desigualdades y la seguridad alimentaria, ayudó a Stratton a conectar con zonas más rurales del estado durante sus años como vicegobernadora.</p><p>Stratton será la cuarta senadora negra de Illinois en el Senado y también la segunda mujer negra en representar al estado. Además, se convierte en la sexta mujer negra en formar parte del actual Senado.</p><p>Stratton venció al líder en recaudación de fondos, el representante federal Raja Krishnamoorthi, a la representante Robin Kelly y a otros ocho candidatos en una primaria reñida que incluyó un repunte tardío en la campaña y millones en apoyo de Pritzker. También fue la primera demócrata en anunciar su candidatura al escaño de Durbin, y anunció el respaldo de Pritzker dos días después.</p><p>Al anunciar su candidatura, Stratton destacó sus logros como vicegobernadora, entre ellos el aumento del salario mínimo, los avances en la infraestructura del estado, las leyes de seguridad de las armas y la consagración de las leyes sobre el aborto en Illinois.</p><p>Los republicanos no han ganado un cargo estatal en Illinois desde hace 12 años, cuando Pritzker derrotó al ex gobernador republicano Bruce Rauner, un estrecho aliado de Tracy. Pero Tracy dijo que se presentó para dar voz a los millones de republicanos del estado.</p><p>Tracy es un abogado y empresario de Springfield. Se desempeñó como presidente del Partido Republicano de Illinois desde 2021 hasta su renuncia en julio de 2024. También fue presidente de la Junta de Juego de Illinois, nombrado en 2015.</p><p>Tracy señaló las peleas internas republicanas como la razón de su salida de la presidencia del partido estatal en 2024, tras tres años y medio, un mandato en el que vio cómo disminuía aún más la influencia del partido en el estado a medida que su base se desplazaba hacia la derecha.</p><p>Tracy se postuló sin éxito para vicegobernador en 2010 y ganó una primaria demócrata para un escaño en el Senado estatal en 2002. Perdió en la elección general.</p><p><i>Sfondeles y Woelfel informaron desde Chicago, Weathersby desde Springfield. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de</i> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: New IHSA bylaw proposals would put public and private schools in separate state tournaments
entries.summary: <p>Until now, the dispute between public and private schools over competitive balance played out in press conferences and postgame interviews. Mount Carmel football coach Jordan Lynch and Batavia football coach Dennis Piron both regularly offered juicy quotes that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/08/19/ihsa-high-school-football-mount-carmel-batavia-private-school" >presented their sides of the issue</a>.</p><p>The time for empty talk has passed. Over the next six weeks, schools across the state will discuss several possible rule changes and state tournament format tweaks that could change the landscape of high school sports in Illinois.</p><p>The ongoing battle between public and private schools over an alleged “private school competitive advantage” is at the center of the two most significant bylaw proposals the Illinois High School Association released on Tuesday. The West Suburban Conference submitted both. The conference includes Downers Grove North and South, Proviso East and West, Hinsdale Central and South, Leyden, Morton, Addison Trail, Willowbrook, York, Lyons, Glenbard West and Oak Park.</p><p>Proposal 8, submitted by the West Suburban, creates separate classes for boundary (public) and non-boundary (private and magnet) schools in the state tournaments. Under this format, public and private schools would no longer compete for the same state championships.</p><p>In four-class sports, there would be three classes for boundary schools and one class for non-boundary schools. In football, there would be six boundary classes and two non-boundary classes.</p><p>Under this proposed system, a basketball state championship game between Young and Glenbard West could not happen. A football state championship game between Maine South and Loyola would be impossible. Each of the schools mentioned would face similar schools and win separate state championships.</p><p>Proposal 15, also submitted by the West Suburban, creates separate paths to the state finals for boundary and non-boundary schools. Boundary and non-boundary schools would have separate sectionals and supersectionals, and one non-boundary team would advance to the state semifinals.</p><p>So basically, only one private/non-boundary public school would be allowed in the state semifinals in each class every year.</p><p>Under this proposed system, schools like Brother Rice, Mount Carmel and Lane would be placed in a separate supersectional, and the winning team would advance directly to the state semifinals in football and basketball. State championships between traditional public schools and non-boundary schools would be possible. Still, only one non-boundary school would be in the state finals in every class and sport.</p><p>Downers Grove North AD Dave Rose, who wrote Proposal 8 and 15, declined to comment specifically on the bylaws, telling the Sun-Times that, “the proposal is still very early in the process, and I'd like to give a chance to be discussed at the town hall meetings in November before talking through it.”</p><p>Athletic directors at Lyons, Hinsdale Central, Downers Grove South and York did not respond to a request for comment.</p><p>According to a source, the West Suburban is expected to listen to feedback at IHSA town hall meetings across the state and then pull back the less popular proposal.</p><p>“St. Laurence and most private schools are in favor of keeping it the way it is,” St. Laurence AD and Catholic League vice president Tim Chandler said. “There are sports where private schools do pretty well and sports where we don’t do well. The focus always seems to be on the sports that the private schools have a good season in.”</p><p>Chandler said that Proposal 8, which separates the private and public schools into different state tournaments, is a non-starter.</p><p>“Private schools would have a decision to make in that situation,” Chandler said. “If we are going to be on our own anyway, would we do it under the IHSA or under our own terms with our own transfer bylaws?”</p><p>“I believe the four best schools should be at state, whether that is private schools or public schools. Restricting access for private schools and guaranteeing one spot doesn’t make sense. There might be sports where four public schools should be at state, and you are taking an opportunity away from a public school by guaranteeing a private school spot.</p><p>“There are a ton of small, non-boundary schools that have no business competing with Mount Carmel and Loyola in sports. That’s not right.”</p><p>Several sources have confirmed to the Sun-Times that the IHSA could push through Proposal 15 without a vote from the schools. Chandler has heard the same, and says the Catholic League would prefer that scenario. The IHSA is believed to prefer keeping private and public schools competing for the same state titles.</p><p>“There has been some talk about the [IHSA board] doing this under board policy instead of it being a bylaw,” Chandler said. “So then the board would have the ability to tweak it a little bit easier. Like what they have done with the current classification stuff. It would be better to see something come through that way.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">What is the best setup for Illinois high school sports state tournaments?</p>— Michael O'Brien (@michaelsobrien) <a href="https://x.com/michaelsobrien/status/2117725297391042886?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p><b>Other notable bylaw proposals:</b></p><p><b>Proposal 0 (already on the ballot):</b> Modifies the multiplier from 1.65 to 2.5. Non-boundary school enrollment will be multiplied by 2.5; this would send private schools and magnet schools into larger classes.</p><p><b>Proposal 2:</b> Increases the percentage of votes needed to pass a bylaw amendment from a simple majority to a 2/3 supermajority. This would make it more difficult to pass new bylaws.</p><p><b>Proposal 12:</b> Modifies transfer eligibility to allow students full eligibility for their first transfer before the start of their sophomore school year. This would basically allow one free transfer with no sitting out during a student’s first year of high school.</p><p><b>Proposal 16:</b> Restores the football setup the state used in 2025-26, rolling back the playoff expansion.</p>

entries.title: Democrat Juliana Stratton takes reins from Dick Durbin in decisive U.S. Senate victory
entries.summary: <p>Juliana Stratton’s fiery anti-President Trump messaging helped to deliver a resounding victory over Republican Don Tracy in the open U.S. Senate seat to replace Sen. Dick Durbin.</p><p>Stratton, 61, has also made history in becoming the second Black woman to represent Illinois in the U.S. Senate.</p><p>"When I became a state representative in 2017, people told me, 'Don't ruffle too many feathers. Don't make too many waves. You're a freshman. Sit back, just learn,'" Stratton said during her victory speech at the Ramova Theatre. "Well, I ignored that advice then. And I certainly won't be sitting back and listening quietly when I get to Washington."</p><p>Stratton vowed to fight "loudly" for affordable healthcare, reproductive freedom, workers' rights and voting rights. She said she'd fight for farmers, caregivers, small businesses, public schools and immigrant communities. And she pledged to represent all Illinoisans, "including those of you who didn't vote for me." </p><p>"Together, we have not only won this seat, but we have won it decisively," Stratton said to a roaring crowd.</p><p>The Associated Press declared Stratton the winner when the polls closed at 7 p.m. With 22% of the vote counted, Stratton led 66.3% to Tracy with 32.3% and independent candidate Whitfield Harrington Jr. at 1.4%.</p><p>The crowd erupted at 7:04 p.m. — moments after the polls closed — as an emcee announced that "it's official" — Stratton will become Illinois' next senator. </p><p>Illinois state Sen. Lakesia Collins said Stratton’s victory “shattered the doubts” and “silenced the skeptics” in order to send a “fearless Black woman to the United States Senate.”</p><p>“Tonight is proof of what happens when you stop doubting, and start trusting, Black women,” Collins said, who added that Stratton is “standing on the shoulders” of former President Barack Obama and Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman ever elected to the Senate.</p><p>Speaking before Stratton's victory speech, Durbin called the duo of Sen. Tammy Duckworth and Stratton "the most powerful team in Washington, D.C." to fight against Trump's agenda.</p><p>In Stratton, Illinois voters chose a progressive voice with a campaign slogan of “F- - - Trump” to take the reins from Durbin, the senior senator who held the seat since 1996. Stratton, Gov. JB Pritzker’s running mate since 2018, repeatedly vowed she’d stand up to the president, and her primary campaign helped to energize voters in a field of 10 candidates.</p><p>Now she’ll bring her progressive platform of abolishing ICE and a push for a $25 minimum wage to Washington alongside five new Democratic colleagues in Congress — part of a new wave of the Illinois congressional delegation after a series of resignations and moves this year.</p><p>Pritzker has downplayed his role in helping Stratton, including a hefty $10 million contribution in the primary campaign which helped her run TV ads. But the governor can now boast that he helped elect a close ally to the U.S. Senate.</p><p>Stratton, a former mediator, was first elected to the Illinois House of Representatives in 2016. As lieutenant governor, she helped lead the Birth Equity Initiative, which addressed the racial disparity in Illinois’ maternal mortality rates for Black women. She also led the Justice, Equity and Opportunity Initiative, with the goal of shifting the state’s criminal legal system toward more restorative programs.</p><p>Her work with the Ag Connects Us All Initiative, which helped to highlight the ways in which the agriculture industry could address inequities and food security, helped Stratton connect to more rural areas of the state in her years as lieutenant governor.</p><p>Stratton will serve as Illinois’ fourth Black senator in the Senate and the second Black woman to represent Illinois. She’s also becoming the sixth Black woman to serve in the current Senate.</p><p>Stratton defeated fundraising leader U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, Rep. Robin Kelly and eight other candidates in a contentious primary that included a late campaign surge and millions in support from Pritzker. She was also the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/04/23/lt-gov-juliana-stratton-candidacy-us-senate-dick-durbin-seat" target="_blank" ><u>first Democrat to announce a bid for Durbin’s seat</u></a>, and announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2025/04/25/pritzker-endorsement-juliana-stratton-senate-seat-dick-durbin" target="_blank" ><u>Pritzker’s endorsement</u></a> just two days later.</p><p>In announcing her bid, Stratton touted her accomplishments as lieutenant governor, including raising the minimum wage, the state’s infrastructure accomplishments, gun safety laws and enshrining abortion laws in Illinois.</p><p>Republicans haven’t won a statewide seat in Illinois in 12 years, when Pritzker unseated GOP former Gov. Bruce Rauner, a close ally of Tracy. But Tracy said he ran to give a voice to the millions of Republicans in the state.</p><p>Tracy is a Springfield attorney and businessman. He served as the chair of the Illinois Republican Party from 2021 until his resignation in July 2024. He is also the former chairman of the Illinois Gaming Board, appointed in 2015.</p><p><i>Sfondeles and Woelfel reported from Chicago; Weathersby reported from Springfield.</i> </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-da0000" name="module-da0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b><u>Race Results</u></b><br><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/governor-illinois-jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-results" >Illinois Governor</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-senate-illinois-midterm-results" >U.S. Senate</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-house-illinois-midterm-results" >4th Congressional District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-state-comptroller-attorney-general-secretary-of-state" >Illinois State Offices</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-illinois-house-97-midterm-results" >Illinois’ 97th House District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-house-midterm-results" >Illinois General Assembly</a></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker beats Darren Bailey for 3rd term, leaving one question: Will he run for president?
entries.summary: <p>Gov. JB Pritzker sailed to a rare third term as Illinois’ chief executive Tuesday with his second consecutive reelection victory over Republican challenger Darren Bailey, lining up the incumbent to become the longest-serving Democratic governor in state history.</p><p>But a quick <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/voter-guide-midterm-election-illinois/illinois-midterm-results-2026/" target="_blank" ><u>election night</u></a> for Pritzker only underscored the question of just how long he intends to stay in the governor’s mansion — and when he might announce a run for president as the 2028 field of contenders takes shape.</p><p>The Associated Press called the race for Pritzker within a minute of the polls closing, just like it did in 2022 when the billionaire governor trounced Bailey, a southern Illinois farmer and former state legislator, by nearly 13 percentage points.</p><p>With less than 8% of the vote counted, Pritzker led with about 67% over Bailey’s 30% and 3% for Collin Corbett, a socially moderate fiscal conservative who mounted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/10/13/jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-illinois-governor-election-november-midterm" target="_blank" ><u>an independent campaign</u></a>.</p><p>With Pritzker’s bottomless campaign resources towering over a fractured Illinois Republican Party, the main question for most Springfield observers after Bailey crushed the field in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/governor-illinois-republican-race-primary-results" target="_blank" ><u>March’s four-way GOP primary</u></a> was whether the hardline conservative challenger could keep his vote deficit from ballooning further in reliably blue Illinois.</p><p>That, along with the question of if — or when — Pritzker will announce a White House bid.</p><p>In front of about a thousand American flag-waving supporters filling the floor of Navy Pier’s Aon Grand Ballroom, the first half of Pritzker’s 19-minute victory speech running down a lengthy list of things he loves about Illinois, from its “horseradish capital of the world” in downstate Collinsville to the White Sox fan it sent to the Vatican.</p><p>But Pritzker soon addressed the presidential elephant in the room.</p><p>“There is one question I have gotten a lot in the last few months: What’s next?” he said. “I’m going to ask you to continue to hope, and to wrap your hope in courage. We climbed one mountain tonight, but we are sitting at the base of another.”</p><p>In a potential preview of a presidential stump speech, Pritzker described “a healthcare system we need to break down to the studs and rebuild” and “an electoral system that needs real campaign finance reform, because no special interest should be able to simply buy the regulations they prefer” — problems that sure sound like they’d best be addressed by a federal office.</p><p>“If you go to work in the morning and come home at night, you ought to make enough money to put food on your table, to see a doctor when you’re sick, to live in a dignified home, to save for retirement and to take a vacation every once in a while,” Pritzker said in front of a packed stage decked with a massive American flag. “We can make that happen, and we must make that happen.”</p><p>Bailey and other Republicans have long accused Pritzker of eyeing his latest reelection as a stepping stone to the White House, an ambition that Pritzker has hardly downplayed.</p><p>Still, Pritzker maintains that he has unfinished business in Springfield after two terms spanning some of the most tumultuous years in state history, from a global pandemic to a chaotic federal deportation campaign and numerous run-ins with the Trump administration.</p><p>Whether or not his focus is solely on his current job, Pritzker becomes the first three-term Illinois governor since Republican Jim Thompson won the third of his record four terms in 1982.</p><p>An heir to the Hyatt hotel fortune, Pritzker used his astronomical financial advantage in the race to remind voters of the state’s 12 credit rating upgrades and a slew of progressive legislative victories he has shepherded through the General Assembly since unseating GOP former Gov. Bruce Rauner in 2018.</p><p>Pritzker’s self-funded, $90 million-plus campaign also blanketed the internet and airwaves with ads painting Bailey as a lackey of Trump, who campaigned alongside Bailey four years ago and endorsed him once again.</p><p>Several dozen people were on hand for Bailey’s election night watch party at an Effingham hotel, many supporters clad in red campaign merchandise and one decked out as a full-on Abraham Lincoln impersonator. Bailey still hadn’t appeared at his party by the time Pritzker finished his victory speech.</p><p>Momentum proved elusive for a campaign that tried to distance itself from Trump, who remains unpopular with voters in Cook County and the collar counties, that once-fertile ground for the Illinois GOP.</p><p>Instead, Bailey labored to keep the focus on concerns around the rising cost of living, which critics can tie to the president’s tariffs and war in Iran; crime, during a year when Chicago has seen <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/morning-edition/2026/09/02/chicago-crime-mayor-brandon-johnson-boeing-mannys-deli" target="_blank" ><u>a historic drop in homicides</u></a>; and the education system, which is heavily reliant on the property taxes that Bailey pledged to cut.</p><p>Pritzker told his supporters they had “vanquished the MAGA Illinois GOP” but also offered Bailey “the blessings of peace in the days ahead: “Let’s commit to work for a time when all our political disputes will be resolved by the better angels of our nature.”</p><p><i>Contributing: Isabela Nieto, WBEZ</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-680000" name="module-680000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><b><u>Race Results</u></b><br><br><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/governor-illinois-jb-pritzker-darren-bailey-collin-corbett-results" >Illinois Governor</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-senate-illinois-midterm-results" >U.S. Senate</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-house-illinois-midterm-results" >4th Congressional District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-state-comptroller-attorney-general-secretary-of-state" >Illinois State Offices</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/us-illinois-house-97-midterm-results" >Illinois’ 97th House District</a> | <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/11/03/illinois-house-midterm-results" >Illinois General Assembly</a></div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Grammy winner Che ‘Rhymefest’ Smith reelected in South Side District 10a Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/10a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 10a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: South Shore, Woodlawn, Greater Grand Crossing, Hyde Park, Kenwood, South Chicago, Douglas, Oakland </i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a>, the Grammy Award-winning hip-hop artist turned activist and politician, sailed to victory Tuesday to keep his seat on the first fully elected Chicago Public Schools board.</p><p>Smith was reelected to the District 10a seat, covering parts of the mid-South Side.</p><p>His only opponent was nonprofit leader <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/tameka-walton/" target="_blank" ><u>Tameka Walton</u></a>, who ran as a write-in candidate after her name was booted off the ballot. Smith far outraised Walton, bringing in nearly three times as much in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a>.</p><p>Stretching from Bronzeville to South Shore, District 10a’s 33 schools include some of the South Side’s most sought-after schools, including Kenwood Academy High School and Murray Language Academy Elementary School, as well as several neighborhood schools that are considered low-performing and have lost enrollment in recent years. A large percentage of students are choosing neighborhood high schools, <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=10a" target="_blank" ><u>according to data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. More than 88% of the students in 10a are Black and nearly 7% are Hispanic.</p><p>When he was elected to the school board two years ago, Smith proudly wore the moniker of an independent after triumphing over candidates with support from the Chicago Teachers Union and the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.</p><p>“I will tell you that my connections in the community got me here, my work got me here,” Smith, a former CPS parent, said before the election. “Money didn't get me here.”</p><p>Unlike in 2024, Smith is now a known entity who has consistently voted against items pushed by the CTU and, for that, has received endorsements and donations from groups that oppose the union. Still, Smith says he would welcome the union’s support and counsel.</p><p>He raised more than $100,000 in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign donations</u></a>, even though his only opponent was a write-in candidate, though Walton picked up CTU’s endorsement. She <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>received donations</u></a> from the CTU PAC and the CTU-affiliated Our Schools PAC.</p><p>Walton said she represented two important constituencies that Smith doesn’t. One, she’s a current mom who had to advocate to get her children into CPS schools where they could thrive. She is also the executive director and founder of a nonprofit that works in schools with children who have experienced trauma.</p><p>“I’m looking beyond how much trouble it was for me to navigate [CPS], but I’m also looking at, as a parent, the things that I want to see done,” she said. “The school should be a safe and welcoming space for both the students and the parents.</p>

entries.title: Juan Ignacio González wins District 8b seat in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/8b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 8b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: New City, Chicago Lawn, Gage Park, McKinley Park, Bridgeport, the Loop, Brighton Park, West Lawn, Near South Side, Armour Square</i></p><p>Juan Ignacio González, a veteran Chicago police detective and local coffee shop owner, defeated college student Alexander Angeles to represent District 8b, a largely Latino area that stretches across the city’s Southwest Side.</p><p>Angeles joined the race as a write-in candidate at the end of August. Earlier this summer, the Chicago election authority kicked <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/07/14/five-school-board-candidates-removed-from-ballot/" target="_blank" ><u>incumbent and Mayor Brandon Johnson appointee Cydney Wallace</u></a> off the ballot due to challenges to her petition signatures.</p><p>González, a Back of the Yards resident, said he was motivated to run for school board in the <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=8b" target="_blank" ><u>mostly Latino district</u></a> after hearing from parents who were concerned about students being used as “political pawns” on May Day. The Chicago Teachers Union and Chicago Public Schools reached an agreement to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/05/01/chicago-public-schools-celebrates-may-day/" target="_blank" ><u>keep schools open on May 1 while allowing civic actions</u></a> after some back-and-forth over whether to call off school for demonstrations.</p><p>“Parents were speaking about some of the challenges and low academic standards we’re facing … and those are issues that I agree with,” González said. “I feel like in my community, there’s no voice for individuals that oftentimes cannot vote or aren’t part of the political system. I was asked to consider it, I looked at the layout, and felt I can help kids in the community.”</p><p>A recent graduate of Hancock College Prep High School and University of Illinois Chicago political science major, Angeles said he ran to be a voice for students, a trait he believes is lacking among board members.</p><p>González was backed by groups that support school choice and oppose the Chicago Teachers Union. His two largest <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a> came from the political arm of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and the Urban Center, which says its mission is to “give voice to a centrist community in Chicago.” Angeles had no donations on file as of Monday.</p><p>There are nearly 25,000 school-aged children in District 8b and nearly three-quarters attend a Chicago public school, according to CPS <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=8b" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. Matching citywide averages, about 59% of students choose neighborhood elementary schools, while 22% choose neighborhood high schools.</p><p>The students enrolled here are primarily Latino, at 68%, while about 19% are Black and 7% are white.</p><p>None of District 8b’s schools received the state’s “exemplary” top rating last year, but 70% ranked at the second-best “commendable” level. Some 9% of the schools received the state’s lowest designation, “intensive,” indicating they remained among the bottom 5% of low-income schools in the state for four years after receiving comprehensive support or continued to have a graduation rate of 67% or below.</p><p><i>Contributing: Francia Garcia Hernandez,</i> <i>Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Brittany Bailey Preston wins South Side District 9a in Chicago School Board race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/9a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 9a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Auburn Gresham, West Englewood, Englewood, New City, Ashburn, Washington Heights </i></p><p>Brittany Bailey Preston, the sole candidate for District 9a, cruised to victory Tuesday night, according to election results from the Associated Press.</p><p>Preston faced no opposition after Angel Velez, who had been appointed by Mayor Brandon Johnson, failed to get on the ballot after a large percentage of his signatures were challenged and invalidated. Preston is married to state Sen. Willie Preston, whose district covers the same neighborhoods she will oversee in her role as a school board member.</p><p>Minutes after being declared the winner, Preston walked into her election watch party at Q’s Lounge in Chicago’s Ashburn neighborhood.</p><p>“I’m feeling well,” she said by phone. “I’m excited to get to work for the children in my community, children in District 9a.”</p><p>Once she starts her term, Preston said she plans to focus on initiatives to raise student’s reading levels, and she wants students to have more options to enroll in trade programs.</p><p>“Our CPS schools should set up students to be successful despite not going to college,” Preston said.</p><p>Also on top of her list: figuring out how to improve lunches for children.</p><p>The majority-Black district includes a mix of 47 neighborhood, charter and magnet schools serving mostly Black and Hispanic students. The area also has one of the lowest percentages of schools that earned either “exemplary” or “commendable” designations last year from the state — the top two ratings — across the city. A number of schools here have struggled with declining enrollment over the past 15 years.</p><p>The district also has one of the lowest percentages citywide of CPS students choosing neighborhood schools. Some 32% of students in 9a chose their neighborhood elementary and high schools compared to 46% systemwide, <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F" target="_blank" ><u>according to data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>.</p><p>This seat was previously held by Frank Thomas, who resigned in June 2025 and was later replaced by Velez. After being removed from the ballot, Velez said he would not pursue a write-in candidacy.</p><p>Preston’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>biggest campaign donation</u></a> came from the SEIU Illinois Council political action committee, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2026/09/21/key-education-endorsements-for-cps-school-board-candidates" target="_blank" ><u>endorsed her</u></a>. Her campaign was also supported by groups who oppose the Chicago Teachers Union and are proponents of school choice and charter schools, including the Urban Center, the Common Ground Collective and the Illinois Network of Charter Schools.</p><p><i>Contributing: Jim Lynch, Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Angel Gutierrez wins District 8a seat in uncontested Chicago School Board race on Far Southwest Side
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/8a/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 8a</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Ashburn, Garfield Ridge, Clearing, West Lawn, Chicago Lawn, West Elsdon</i></p><p>Nonprofit leader <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/angel-gutierrez/" target="_blank" ><u>Angel Gutierrez</u></a> has unsurprisingly retained his Far Southwest Side school board seat in an uncontested race.</p><p>Gutierrez, who lives in Garfield Ridge, was <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-8-gutierrez-ponce" target="_blank" ><u>first elected to the school board in 2024</u></a> to represent a heavily Hispanic district on the Far Southwest Side. This election cycle he picked up support from the Service Employees International Union, which represents thousands of support staff at Chicago Public Schools, and pro-charter school groups. But no candidates filed paperwork to oppose him.</p><p>Gutierrez said his first priorities when he gets sworn into office in January will be figuring out the CPS budget for the short and long term.</p><p>“We got to get our fiscal house in order, number one,” Gutierrez said in an interview after being declared the winner Tuesday. “We need to put into practice and bring fruition to [CPS CEO/Supt. Macquline] King’s committee for financing our schools. We need to figure out the continuous not having enough money over the past two years.”</p><p>Even though he ran unopposed, Gutierrez said he’s grateful to all the district voters and the groups that endorsed him.</p><p>Overall, students in this district are more likely to attend their neighborhood schools than in other communities. For elementary school, 69% of students attend their neighborhood schools compared to 56% citywide. For high school, 28% of students in District 8a choose a local school, compared to 23% citywide, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>.</p><p>The area has leaned more conservative than other parts of the city and is home to more families than single-person households. In 2023, voters here heavily favored mayoral candidate Paul Vallas, a former Chicago Public Schools CEO, over Mayor Brandon Johnson, a former Chicago Teachers Union organizer. In 2024, most precincts favored Donald Trump for president.</p><p>Gutierrez said leading up to the election that he wants to improve special education, increase opportunities to learn skilled trades, and ensure access to reliable transportation, including school buses — proposals he said would benefit students attending their neighborhood schools.</p><p>Gutierrez also said he supports continuing the CPS strategy of allowing families to choose from a range of schools outside their neighborhood.</p><p>The political action committees of the Illinois Network of Charter Schools and SEIU <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>donated to Gutierrez’ campaign</u></a> even though he was running uncontested.</p><p>He was also the only board member calling for the state to opt into the Trump administration’s federal tax credit scholarship program, which offers a tax credit for donations made to organizations that grant scholarships for students to attend private schools or to pay for other education needs. Illinois has not agreed to participate.</p><p>Gutierrez sends his children to a Catholic school.</p><p><b><i>Contributing:</i></b><i> Francia Garcia Hernandez, Block Club Chicago</i></p>

entries.title: Mondelez sues candy brand Joyride over Sour Patch Kids dupe
entries.summary: <p>The West Loop-based maker of Sour Patch Kids said a rival candy brand is copying its popular kid-shaped gummy candy and signature packaging, according to a lawsuit filed Monday in the Northern District of Illinois.</p><p>Mondelēz Global, which also owns snack brands like Oreo and Ritz, described Texas-based Joyride as "a well-funded, private equity-backed candy company who wasn’t making friends on its own. So it stole SOUR PATCH KIDS’ popular look, and dared Mondelēz to do something about it." </p><p>In April 2025, Joyride released "Sour Smacks," brightly colored chewy candies in the shape of grinning people inside yellow-and-green packaging. </p><p>Mondelēz said in its complaint that the candy's design and package is a copy of its iconic kid-shaped gummies and yellow-and-green packaging. It also said Joyride announced a social media campaign in January 2025 to “usurp and surpass” Sour Patch Kids’ popularity by drawing more online followers. </p><p>Joyride Chief Creative Officer and co-owner Ryan Trahan posted on Instagram that he planned to make the company the most followed candy brand on the platform — a title the official Sour Patch Kids' Instagram acc</p><p>ount held, the suit said. Trahan, 28, is also a YouTube personality with more 24 million subscribers.</p><p>"Joyride’s strategy to associate itself with SOUR PATCH KIDS was successful: according to Joyride, its posts 'went viral,' supposedly gained Joyride 'over 300,000 followers,' and induced other major retail brands to comment on Joyride’s posts," according to the lawsuit.</p><p>Mondelēz and Joyride didn't respond to a request for comment.</p><p>Founded in 2008 as Project 7, the company rebranded in 2022 to Joyride and hired Trahan. Its products are sold at retailers like Target and Walmart, as well as online. </p><p>Joyride's sour gummy candy and Sour Patch Kids are often sold at the same retailers and on the same shelf, the lawsuit said.</p><p>The company also disclosed in a May 2025 securities filing that it raised $30 million in private equity funding, valuing Joyride at about $100 million. </p><p>Mondelēz said Joyride was able to raise funds because the brand increasingly associated itself with Sour Patch Kids. The complaint cited Joyride's 2020 and 2022 sour candy packaging, which had different names, candy shape and packaging.</p><p>The food manufacturing giant is seeking permanent injunctive relief to entries.title: Ellen Rosenfeld wins North Side District 4b Chicago School Board seat in uncontested race
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/4b/" target="_blank" ><i><u>District 4b</u></i></a><i> neighborhoods: Lincoln Park, North Center, Lake View, Logan Square</i></p><p>As the lone school board candidate in her North Side area, incumbent Ellen Rosenfeld easily won another term representing District 4b, according to Associated Press election results.</p><p>Though Rosenfeld, a former Chicago Public Schools teacher and district engagement specialist, had no opponents, she took in more than $100,000 in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a>, mostly from individuals — and more than several school board candidates in competitive races.</p><p>Rosenfeld first <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/chicago-school-board/2024/11/05/election-results-district-4-zaccor-rosenfeld-brown-day-gioiosa-davis" target="_blank" ><u>won her seat handily in 2024</u></a> against five other would-be school board members in the city’s most crowded race. That year, pro-school choice groups spent heavily to back her and oppose a teachers union-backed candidate.</p><p>She’s made serving on the board her full-time role the past two years after leaving her position with CPS Family and Community Engagement.</p><p>Rosenfeld is part of a bloc of seven elected members who have opposed the mayor’s appointees and elected allies on the board, who make up a majority. She has backing from the Service Employees International Union Illinois State Council, which represents CPS support staff, and other groups that oppose the Chicago Teachers Union, the mayor’s former employer and key ally. As of last week, she’d received a notable $100,000 in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-campaign-finance/" target="_blank" ><u>campaign contributions</u></a>, mostly from individuals, though she was the only candidate on the ballot.</p><p>The former local school council chair and mother of four CPS graduates argues the current board has been too mired in politics and susceptible to outside pressure. But she feels the incoming fully elected board could preside over an academic resurgence, from a rise in reading proficiency to a decrease in chronic absenteeism, one of her key concerns. She said the next board must rally around a set of goals for improving the district.</p><p>“Without a shared vision, it’s almost impossible to get the good stuff done,” Rosenfeld said.</p><p>District 4b is home to 18 schools, including several high-performing neighborhood schools, coveted magnets and a popular selective-enrollment high school, Lane Tech College Prep. Families here choose their neighborhood schools at higher rates than in many other school board districts.</p><p>The school board district serves a significantly higher percentage of white students than the district as a whole. About 46% of students are white, 25% are Hispanic, 12% are Black and 9% are Asian American, according to <a class="Link" href="https://projects.chalkbeat.org/2026/chicago-school-board-election-map/?loader=true&initialWidth=690&windowHeight=501&parentTitle=Chicago%2520school%2520board%2520election%25202026%2520voter%2520guide%253A%2520District%252010a%2520candidates%2520-%2520Chalkbeat&parentUrl=https%253A%252F%252Fwww.chalkbeat.org%252Fchicago%252F2026%252F09%252F24%252Fschool-board-election-2026-district-10a-candidates-voter-guide%252F#districtNumber=4b" target="_blank" ><u>data compiled by Chalkbeat</u></a>. District 4b also has the highest share of schools that <a class="Link" href="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/SVkXB/1/index.html" target="_blank" ><u>received the state’s top rating of “exemplary</u></a>” for academic performance last year.</p>

entries.title: Miami is No. 1 in first CFP rankings; Indiana is fourth with Notre Dame at No. 11
entries.summary: <p>It's been a confusing college football season so far. Nobody felt that more deeply than the College Football Playoff selection committee, which raised eyebrows galore in its first attempt of the season to make sense of it all.</p><p>Undefeated Miami received top billing in the committee's first crack at the CFP rankings Tuesday, followed by Georgia and undefeated Utah.</p><p>From there, the 13 people in that room could have been picking from a hat. Defending champion Indiana (8-1) was ranked fourth — eight spots ahead of Ohio State (6-2), which beat the Hoosiers 19-15 last month but has since lost quarterback Julian Sayin.</p><p>At No. 5 was Alabama (6-2) — eight spots ahead of Tennessee (6-2), even though the Tide is only a few weeks removed from a 16-point loss to the Vols. At No. 6 was Kentucky (7-1), followed by Texas (6-2).</p><p>UCLA, the nation's only other undefeated team, was ranked eighth.</p><p>Oh, and Notre Dame. The Irish (7-1) were ranked 11th — seven spots lower than their spot in the AP Top 25 — and that ranking brought with it a simple message: As the last team that would make the bracket if the playoffs started today, they need to beat Miami on Saturday or risk slipping due to a schedule that clearly did not impress the committee.</p><p>"A very, very good football team," committee chair Hunter Yurachek said of Notre Dame. "But when you look at Notre Dame's schedule and the wins they have versus the teams ahead of them, they don't have that signature win right now."</p><p>In fact, Notre Dame's biggest game so far resulted in its only loss — 28-24 at BYU two weeks ago.</p><p>Ohio State was ranked 12th, but would be on the outside looking in because Boise State, ranked 25th, would get the Group of Six automatic bid.</p><p>It would have been easy — maybe too easy — to blame the Buckeyes' fall on the fact that their offense is now in the hands of a freshman quarterback, Luke Fahey. But Yurachek said the committee was more concerned with Ohio State's defense in its 30-18 loss to a 20th-ranked USC team that hasn't impressed anyone so far.</p><p>Regarding the gap between the Hoosiers and Buckeyes — and the Crimson Tide and Volunteers — Yurachek brought up a blast from last year that confused most everyone: Head-to-head comparisons don't come into play unless the teams are in the same four-team "pod," i.e., 1-4, 5-8, 9-12.</p><p>"Yes, they had that loss to Tennessee," Yurachek said of the Tide. "But Tennessee doesn't have that same level of quality wins. Yes, they beat Alabama, but you have to go deeper" to find its next-best win.</p><p>Meanwhile, he said, the Tide got lots of love in the selection room for a win against Mississippi State in September before the Bulldogs disintegrated with the injury to QB Kamario Taylor. Mississippi State is currently 2-4.</p><p></p><h3>The rankings</h3><p>1. Miami 8-0</p><p>2. Georgia 7-1</p><p>3. Utah 8-0</p><p>4. Indiana 8-1</p><p>5. Alabama 6-2</p><p>6. Kentucky 7-1</p><p>7. Texas 6-2</p><p>8. UCLA 8-0</p><p>9. BYU 7-1</p><p>10. Mississippi 6-2</p><p>11. Notre Dame 7-1</p><p>12. Ohio State 6-2</p><p>13. Tennessee 6-2</p><p>14. LSU 6-2</p><p>15. Texas Tech 7-1</p><p>16. Wake Forest 7-1</p><p>17. Houston 6-2</p><p>18. Missouri 6-2</p><p>19. Iowa 6-2</p><p>20. Southern Cal 7-2</p><p>21. South Carolina 5-3</p><p>22. Arizona 6-2</p><p>23. Oregon 5-3</p><p>24. Florida 5-3</p><p>25. Boise State 7-1</p><p>The four highest-ranked teams determined by the selection committee will be seeded Nos. 1-4 and receive a first-round bye. Seeds 5-12 will play each other in the first round.</p>

entries.title: U.S. Army rep: Helicopters not hit by fireworks during Bears-Seahawks flyover (VIDEO)
entries.summary: <p>SEATTLE — Videos of Black Hawk helicopters flying over Lumen Field on Monday before <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a>’ game against the Seahawks caused alarm because of what looked like a close call between the aircraft and stadium fireworks, but a representative from the U.S. Army said there was no issue during the flyover.</p><p>The four helicopters flew over the field during the national anthem, and fireworks shot out of the north end zone as they did.</p><p>Lt. Col. Cynthia Holuta from nearby Joint Base Louis-McChord <a class="Link" href="https://komonews.com/news/local/fireworks-appear-to-hit-military-helicopter-during-pregame-flyover-lumen-field-seattle-seahawks-game-blackhawk-chopper" target="_blank" >told KOMO</a>, the ABC affiliate in Seattle, “We can confirm that no fireworks struck the aircraft, no aircraft were damaged, and no members of the aircrew were injured," Holuta said.</p><p>Here’s a video of the scene:</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">New video obtained by <a href="https://x.com/komonews?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@komonews</a> shows fireworks being set off from Lumen Field during pregame festivities last night - right as several military helicopters passed by. <br><br>JBLM tells us no helicopters were hit by the fireworks. <a href="https://t.co/GD5FaG8HCR">pic.twitter.com/GD5FaG8HCR</a></p>— Steve McCarron KOMO (@SteveTVNews) <a href="https://x.com/SteveTVNews/status/2117706489641210027?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">November 3, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>There was no indication in real-time of any danger or incident at Lumen Field, and the game proceeded on time. The Bears stormed to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/11/02/bears-big-plan-coming-together-beautifully-as-34-17-win-over-seahawks-pushes-them-to-best-start-since-2012" >a 34-17 win</a> over the defending champions for arguably their most impressive win of coach Ben Johnson’s tenure.</p>
